# Store#forEach and Collection#findBy copy all items on every iteration

## Context

I found this while profiling Memory Core's `mark_read` drain today (neo-agent-brain#464). 6.6 GB of that drain's allocation sat in the generic config getter's legacy array copy.

The engine's own collections read the same getter. `collection.Base` declares `items_` as `{clone: 'shallow', value: null}` without a `cloneOnGet`, so every `collection.items` read returns a fresh copy. Measured: `c.items !== c.items`. One read of a 100k collection costs about 0.067 ms, against about 0.00013 ms for `getCount()`.

## The Problem

Two core loops read that getter once per iteration, so their cost grows quadratically:
- `Neo.collection.Base#findBy` reads `me.items[i]` inside its loop, twice on a match.
- `Neo.data.Store#forEach` passes `me.items` as the callback's fourth argument on every iteration.

Measured on `dev@202699d10c` with a unit probe whose callback does nothing:

| n | `Collection#findBy` | `Store#forEach` | plain `getAt` loop |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1,000 | 1 ms | 1 ms | 0 ms |
| 10,000 | 13 ms | 13 ms | 2 ms |
| 50,000 | 1,802 ms | 1,876 ms | 10 ms |

The engine's callers are `list.Base` (while rendering), `tree.List` (three sites), `tree.Accordion` (two), and the list and tree drag zones. It is invisible at today's typical sizes, but at 50k records a single call blocks the App worker for about 1.9 s.

## The Architectural Reality

- The generated config getter in `src/Neo.mjs` has no `cloneOnGet` for `items`, so it takes the legacy branch: `Array.isArray(value)` leads to `value.slice()`.
- `collection.Base` already reads its backing array as `me._items` wherever it must not copy, 22 times in all.
- `data.Store#findBy` delegates to `super.findBy` and maps the results to Records.

## The Fix

- `Collection#findBy`: iterate the backing `_items` array, not the getter.
- `Store#forEach`: take one copy of `items` before the loop and pass it on every call. The fourth argument stays a defensive copy, but there is now one copy per call instead of one per record.
- Red-first unit cases count `items` getter reads per call, so the test does not rely on timings.

Decision Record impact: none.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] AC-1 A unit case shows that `Collection#findBy` over n items reads the `items` getter zero times, and that `Store#forEach` reads it once per call. Both cases are red on `dev` (n reads).
- [ ] AC-2 Rerun on the 50k probe, `findBy` and `forEach` each finish within 5× of the plain `getAt` loop. The receipt goes in the PR.
- [ ] AC-3 The full unit suite is green.

## Out of Scope

- The getter's copy itself. Giving `items` a non-copying `cloneOnGet` changes a public contract, since callers may rely on a copy they can mutate.
- Single reads such as `me.items.length`, which cost O(n) per call, not per iteration.

## Contract Ledger (added for PR #19193's review)

| Target surface | Source of authority | Behavior after the fix | Fallback | Docs | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `Neo.collection.Base#findBy(fn, scope, start, end)` | the method | Iterates the backing `_items`, re-read on every iteration, so the collection's current state stays visible to the callback. It returns the matching items as before. | — | JSDoc unchanged | `MassiveData.spec.mjs`: 0 getter reads per call (110 on `dev`) |
| `Neo.data.Store#forEach(fn, scope)`, called back as `fn(record, index, items)` | the method | `items` is one defensive copy, shared by all the callbacks of a call: (1) every entry the loop has reached is its Record (`items[index] === record`, lazy hydration included); (2) a callback that changes the store's count gets a fresh copy from the next call on; (3) mutating `items` never reaches the store. | — | JSDoc on `forEach` ("treat it as read-only") | `Store.spec.mjs` "forEach callback items": 3 cases, green on `dev`, red on a plain one-copy version. `MassiveData.spec.mjs`: 1 getter read per call when the count is unchanged. |

The one intentional change from `dev`: `dev` gave every call its own fresh copy, so a callback mutating `items` only affected its own copy. Now the copy is shared across calls, so treat it as read-only.
